text: This lab puts a real monthly budget through the full set of cost levers from this chapter — device choice, program-set batching, and shot-budget sizing — and checks whether a proposed workload actually fits inside it.

Start with a five-thousand-dollar monthly budget, split across dev, staging, and production. Dev gets the smallest share, fifteen percent, since most development runs on free simulators. Staging gets twenty-five percent for real-hardware integration testing. Production gets sixty percent, weighted heaviest since it's the revenue-generating usage — and that split alone buys twenty-four real confirmation tasks a month for development.
This real console is where every dollar of that allocation actually gets spent, month after month — the same dashboard behind every pricing decision this chapter has walked through.

Now the workload check. A daily VQE recalibration job, a hundred fifty iterations, batched, two thousand shots per evaluation on Rigetti Ankaa-3, comes out to thirty dollars ninety cents per iteration. Per day: four thousand six hundred thirty-five dollars. Per month, running twenty-two business days: a hundred one thousand nine hundred seventy dollars. That workload does not fit a three-thousand-dollar production budget — it exceeds it by roughly thirty-four times.
This is the real form where a budget decision like that one actually becomes an enforced ceiling, not just a number on a spreadsheet nobody checks.

And here's that ceiling, live, on a real per-device basis. Cutting shots from two thousand to five hundred, and running weekly instead of daily, together bring that number down by roughly twenty times — still probably short of the original target, which means the honest next step is re-scoping the frequency or precision requirement with the actual stakeholder, backed by this arithmetic, not silently overspending or silently degrading quality to force a fit.

That closes out cost, latency, and resource management. Chapter 5 is one continuous capstone project across four lessons: scope it, build it, harden it with error handling and cost tracking, and review the finished architecture like an engineer.
